newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Labuan reports sharp growth in '96.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Labuan reports sharp growth in '96.

text.p: The number of banks and insurance companies in Malaysia's tax haven on Labuan island grew sharply last year, the Labuan Offshore Financial Services Authority (LOFSA) said on Wednesday.

Companies registering as offshore entities also rose, LOFSA, the island's regulatory authority said in its 1996 annual report. The total number of offshore companies is expected to increase to 1,500 by the end of 1997 from 979 at present.
"In terms of company incorporation, what was achieved in 1996 was almost as many as the number achieved in the previous five years," it said.
Enactment of new laws in 1996 and more legislation awaiting approval in parliament this year would provide fresh impetus for growth this year, the report said.
Malaysia has been promoting Labuan island, located off the coast of Borneo in the South China Sea, as an international offshore financial centre (IOFC) since 1990.
The governing authority for the IOFC said deposits of the 52 offshore banks in Labuan rose by 79 percent to $4.31 billion at the end of 1996 against $2.41 billion a year before.
Loan outstandings of these banks grew by 42.8 percent to $11.96 billion in 1996 over the previous year.
"Although 71 percent of loans at the end of 1996 were still for residents (Malaysians), it was significantly lower than the percentage at the end of 1995 (83.7 percent)," LOFSA said.
Similarly, Malaysians' share of the total deposits at 63.7 percent at the end of 1996 was much lower than 78.7 percent at the end of the previous year, it said.
LOFSA said borrowings from their respective head offices and other branches accounted for 51.8 percent of funding for the offshore banks. Deposits accounted for another 25.8 percent of the resources.
It said pre-tax profit for the 52 banks in 1996 rose by 73.2 percent to a total of $132.5 million.
The 11 offshore insurance companies in Labuan reported their assets more than tripled to $138.2 million at the end of last year, the LOFSA annual report said.
The insurance firms' gross premium increased to $35.8 million last year from $6.4 million in 1995, it said.
LOFSA said it was trying to develop Labuan as a complete "supermarket of offshore financial services" with Islamic instruments as its niche.

In order to do that "LOFSA reviewed the existing legislation in order to make the necessary regulatory changes to facilitate the expansion and deepen the offshore financial services industry", it said.
